en: The Hundred Gates into the Ocean of Meaning of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, with Preface, composed by the Śramaṇa Fazang of Jianfu Monastery in the Capital.

Preface to the Hundred Gates into the Ocean of Meaning of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra: Now, dependent origination is inconceivable; it truly pervades all things. The Dharma-realm is unfathomable; it truly manifests...
Manifesting throughout the ten directions, there is nowhere where the ocean of nature is not harmoniously integrated; responding to the capacities of sentient beings, it reveals the One.
The brilliant radiance of wisdom shines upon the world, thereby penetrating the Three.
The sublime and subtle words manifest the Perfect Teaching upon a single fine hair;
the wondrous and holy assembly reveals their entire bodies within a speck of dust.
This utterly transcends the limits of conceptual thought.
Transcending the bounds of famous sayings,
I have humbly observed that the profound guiding principles are vast and deep,
while their wondrous purport is subtle and ineffable.
Those who peruse it find it difficult to exhaust its source;
those who study it rarely reach its ultimate limit.
Consequently, these subtle words remain stagnant within the mind.
It constantly serves as the field for objective contemplation;
yet the ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi) resides right before one's eyes,
yet is instead inverted into the realm of names and signs (nāma-rūpa).
Now, it comprehensively gathers the profound mysteries and encompasses the great tradition;
it brings forth the sutra scrolls from amidst the dust of the world.
The Wheel of Dharma was turned within a single pore;
for the enlightened, their virtue flourishes on that very day,
while for the ignorant, their hope is cut off for many lifetimes.
If one grasps its underlying intent, even mountains and peaks can be moved;
if one deviates from its essential meaning, even a grain of dust is difficult to enter.
Thus, upon a single mote of dust—
Revealing their true virtues,
one exhausts this ocean of nature and surveys that forest of practice.
Ten gates are presented in general,
while a hundred meanings are opened up in detail;
they interpenetrate yet remain unmixed.
The single limit is resplendent;
the meaning shines brilliantly upon the titles,
and the principle is clearly manifest within the words.
It is hoped that those who have entered the Way will gain a rough understanding of its essential principles through these enumerated categories.

The sections are arranged as follows: Chapter One: The Gate of Dependent Origination Conforming to Quiescence Chapter Two: The Gate of the Ultimate Reality Withdrawing its Traces Chapter Three: The Gate of the Universal Radiance of All-Knowledge Chapter Four: The Gate of Melted Fusion and Spontaneous Functioning Chapter Five: The Gate of the Manifestation of Essence and Function Chapter Six: The Gate of the Manifestation of Differentiation Chapter Seven: The Gate of Cultivation, Study, and Perfect Accomplishment Chapter Eight: The Gate of Attaining Benefits through Antidotes Chapter Nine: The Gate of the Opening and Closing of Essence and Function Chapter Ten: The Gate of Decisive Selection and Accomplishment Chapter One: The Gate of Dependent Origination Conforming to Quiescence Now, regarding the myriad phenomena of dependent origination:
Existence must be manifested through many gates;
the doctrine of non-substantiality is a single principle.
A doctrine is surely revealed through its manifold virtues.
If one divides its power and function,
the significance of its contraction and expansion becomes easy to understand; if one surveys its profound guiding principle, [the truth is revealed].
Thus, the gateway to principle and phenomena will finally be clarified.
Now, speaking in terms of essence and function,
we shall briefly distinguish ten meanings.

First, clarifying dependent origination; second, entering the Dharma-realm; third, realizing non-arising; fourth, contemplating signlessness; fifth, understanding formation and destruction; sixth, manifesting concealment and appearance; seventh, generating bodhicitta; eighth, opening up nirvana; ninth, investigating coming and going; tenth, mirroring movement and stillness. First, regarding the clarification of dependent origination:
Just as when one perceives an object,
that object is a manifestation of one's own mind; it exists by virtue of being a manifestation of one's own mind.
It immediately serves as a condition for one's own mind;
through the presence of that condition,
mental factors then arise.
Therefore, objects are called "dharmas arisen from conditions.
As the Sūtra says:
"All dharmas arise from conditions."
Without conditions, there is no arising;
the causes and conditions for sinking into samsara do not exist externally.
Ultimately, there are no phenomena external to the mind that can serve as conditions for it;
even when one discriminates objects, [they do not exist apart from the mind].
Nor is it an object of grasping;
rather, this appearance of a single atom as being round and small arises based upon the dharmas.
Provisionally established as if existing,
they ultimately lack substantial reality;
they cannot be apprehended upon examination.
Renunciation cannot be apprehended.
Since there is nothing to be grasped or renounced,
one thereby knows.
The substance of sensory objects is empty and non-existent;
now one realizes that conditions are not truly conditions,
and there is no arising that is not wondrous.
Yet the substance of dependent origination is quiescent;
its arising is eternally non-arising.
To penetrate its substance is to follow conditions.
That which does not arise yet constantly arises—
seeing it thus is called true knowledge and vision.
Regarding the second, entering the dharma-realm:
even a single minute speck of dust is a phenomenon arising through dependent origination.
The Dharma manifests in accordance with wisdom;
its functions differ,
yet it is the dharma of this realm.
Because they lack inherent nature, they have no boundaries;
their non-dual characteristics merge and become identical with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Equal in extent to the realm of empty space, it pervades all things;
appearing in every place, there is nowhere it is not clearly manifest.
Yet, this single mote of dust—
They do not know one another among all phenomena,
nor do they see one another. Why is this?
Since each and every one is entirely the perfectly complete *dharmadhātu*,
universally encompassing all without any further separate *dharmadhātu*,
there is therefore no further mutual knowing or mutual seeing.
Even if one speaks of knowledge and vision,
let it not be anything other than the knowledge and vision of the dharma-realm;
for ultimately, there is no separate dharma-realm that can be known or seen.
The Sūtra says:
"In the dharma-realm there is no dharma-realm;
the dharma-realm does not know the dharma-realm."
If intrinsic nature and characteristics do not exist,
then it is the dharma-dhātu of principle;
yet phenomena remain unimpeded and manifest in their full detail.
This matter is the Dharma-realm;
it accords with principle and phenomena without obstruction,
being two yet non-dual.
Non-duality is itself duality;
this is the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
As for those who have attained the threefold penetration of non-arising:
That is to say, the sensory object is the condition for the mind,
and the mind is the cause of the sensory object;
thus, cause and condition come together in harmony.
Illusory appearances arise only from conditions;
because they arise dependently,
they necessarily lack intrinsic nature.
Why is this? For now, objects do not perceive themselves;
they must necessarily depend upon the mind.
The mind is not self-existent;
it also depends upon conditions.
Because they depend upon one another, [the mind arises].
Thus, there is no fixed dependence on conditions for arising;
because there is no fixed dependence on conditions for arising,
it is called non-arising.
It is not that dependent origination is said to be non-arising;
as the treatise states:
"Causes do not arise from themselves."
Because they arise dependently,
that which arises through conditions does not arise of itself;
because they arise from causes.
Birth now arises through conditions;
only then can it be called "birth. To realize that birth has no intrinsic nature—this is true understanding.
This is precisely non-arising.
Yet arising and non-arising mutually establish and mutually negate one another.
If it is negated, there is no arising;
if it is established, it arises through conditions.
This is because establishment and negation occur simultaneously.
Therefore, at the time of arising, there is no arising.
One who understands in this way is said to have realized non-arising.
Fourth, regarding the contemplation of signlessness:
for example, the circular and minute appearance of a single speck of dust is a false construct arising from the transformations of one's own mind; it has no reality.
Now, since it cannot be grasped,
we know that the characteristics of sensory objects are empty and non-existent.
Arising from the mind,
it is understood to be devoid of intrinsic nature;
this is called "signlessness."
The Sūtra says:
"The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty;
there is not even the slightest mark."
Although characteristics cannot be apprehended even when grasped,
the meaning of "non-existence" is not negated;
for it is precisely because characteristics lack intrinsic nature that dharmas are established.
Taking the Dharma as an assistant to the signless is because one does not lose the characteristic of the Dharma; thus,
the characteristic is itself the non-characteristic, and the non-characteristic is itself the characteristic.
Marks and the absence of marks are,
in reality, without distinction.
This is the meaning of the absence of marks.
Just as with a snake on a rope,
one should know that it is said to be entirely without a snake.
The rope is the basis for the non-existent snake;
now, this Dharma is the Dharma of signlessness.
It takes the Dharma itself entirely as the mark of signlessness.
Regarding the fifth point, the completion of arising and destruction:
for example, when atoms arise and are established through conditions, this is "arising";
that the very substance does not remain as an atom is "destruction."
Now, by discerning conditions as non-conditions,
they are termed "conditioned-arising";
by discerning destruction as non-destruction.
This is called the destruction of conditions.
Since this destruction does not obstruct the initial formation of a phenomenon,
the moment of destruction is precisely the moment of formation.
Because it is established through non-existence,
the very moment of its establishment is precisely the moment of its destruction.
All are established simultaneously;
there is neither before nor after.
If there is no disintegration, then there is formation.
This exists by way of intrinsic nature;
if that which is established were to perish,
it would be a nihilistic emptiness.
The boundaries of formation and destruction are one;
their characteristics manifest through mutual dependence.
Sixth, the demonstration of concealment and manifestation:
When one observes that the characteristics of objects cannot be apprehended,
then those characteristics are exhausted and emptiness manifests;
this is because when one perceives characteristics, one does not yet accord with the ultimate principle.
Therefore, while the phenomena are manifest, their underlying principle remains hidden.
Furthermore, these objects and all dharmas mutually support and encompass one another.
Existence and non-existence differ.
If the dust can subsume that [object],
then that becomes hidden while this becomes manifest.
If that [consciousness] can subsume the sensory objects,
then the objects become hidden and that [consciousness] becomes manifest;
their concealment and manifestation share a single boundary.
Now, by merely manifesting time,
that which was hidden is established. Why is this?
Through the manifestation of the whole during the time of concealment, it becomes manifest;
through the concealment of the whole during the time of manifestation, it becomes concealed.
Thus, characteristics are established by way of mutual dependence.
Therefore, when it is concealed, it is precisely manifest; when it is manifest, it is precisely concealed.
Regarding the seven types of those who awaken to bodhi:
This means that these very objects are quiescent nirvana and devoid of intrinsic nature; they are the Buddha’s bodhi because they are manifested by wisdom.
Now, by thoroughly comprehending the principle that all sentient beings, objects, hairs, and so forth are devoid of intrinsic nature, [one realizes this].
Because one attains the wisdom of the Buddha’s bodhi,
within the body of the Buddha’s bodhi,
one perceives all sentient beings attaining perfect enlightenment and turning the wheel of Dharma.
Furthermore, because sentient beings, as well as atoms, hairs, and so forth,
are entirely constituted by the principle of the Buddha’s bodhi,
they exist within the bodhi-body of sentient beings.
Upon seeing the Buddha, one generates the bodhicitta and cultivates the practices of a bodhisattva;
one should know that there is no view other than this regarding the Buddha’s bodhi.
Now, the Buddha transforms sentient beings within the realm of dust,
and these sentient beings in turn receive the Buddha’s transformation within that same realm of dust;
therefore, the Buddha is the Buddha of sentient beings.
Sentient beings are precisely the sentient beings of the Buddha;
although there may be opening and closing,
in the end there is no difference.
One who perceives in this way is said to have awakened the bodhicitta and give rise to great compassion of identical essence.
This refers to the transformation and edification of sentient beings.
Eighth, regarding the opening of *nirvāṇa*:
this means that failing to understand that defilements are manifestations of delusion constitutes birth.
Furthermore, one perceives that the obscuration of sensory objects and the obscuration of delusion constitute cessation;
thus, based on the characteristics of flux, arising, and ceasing,
one conditions these upon the sensory objects.
The deluded mind arises through transformation,
claiming this to be real;
now one seeks the characteristics of arising and ceasing.
Ultimately, there is no place of arising,
nor is anything to be obtained;
with the movement of thought, it vanishes of its own accord.
When all false imaginings are extinguished,
that place of extinction is called Great Nirvana.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"Cyclic wandering is birth and death;
immovability is named nirvana."
Ninth, regarding the examination of coming and going:
when a particle of dust moves eastward with the wind,
the characteristic of "going" cannot be apprehended.
When they come from the west with the wind,
even their appearance of coming cannot be apprehended;
they are all merely dharmas of dust.
Ultimately, there is no characteristic of coming or going,
because they lack substantial reality;
when they come, they come from nowhere.
When departing, there is likewise nothing that departs.
As the Sūtra says:
"Dharmas have neither coming nor going."
Because they never abide.
It is precisely because one realizes that the coming and going of objects has no substantial essence;
therefore, coming and going are themselves the absence of coming and going.
Without coming or going, it constantly comes and goes;
established as a single limit,
there is no distinction between self and other.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"The Bodhisattva comes with the characteristic of non-coming;
he goes with the characteristic of non-going."
Therefore, without moving from the realm of dust,
one reaches the ten directions;
yet one is never separate from the ten directions.
Yet, while entering the realms of sensory dust,
they never truly come or go;
such is the measure of their coming and going.
It is equal to the Dharma-realm.
Regarding the tenth point, "discerning movement and stillness":
this refers to how sensory objects drift and flutter with the wind.
This movement is quiescent and does not arise; this is stillness.
Now, at the time of stillness, movement is not extinguished;
thus, stillness is entirely constituted by movement.
Now, at the time of movement, it does not cease due to stillness;
thus, movement is entirely constituted by stillness.
This is because they mutually constitute one another as a complete whole.
Therefore, when there is movement, it is precisely stillness;
when there is stillness, it is precisely movement.
It is just as wind, though inherently unmoving, is able to move all things.
If there were motion prior [to the entity], it would lose its own essence;
consider this: it could not move again.
However, since the aforementioned meanings of dependent origination have already been established,
it is logically inconsistent to isolate all phenomena as being individually exhausted and then encompass them collectively to form a totality that is inexhaustible.
If one seeks its profundity,
though it occupies a narrow space, it is ever expansive;
if one wishes to fathom its abyss...
Even if one dwells in the profound, it remains increasingly shallow;
how vast indeed is the meaning of dependent origination! 2.
The Second Gate: The Actual Reality Withdraws Its Traces. Now, when returning to the great abyss of the ultimate source, there is no longer any "pouring in" from the hundred rivers.
When the true source is stilled, conditions dissolve to form the myriad existents; thus,
the various streams vanish and their characteristics are exhausted,
and as manifold conditions become still, all phenomena are empty.
Returning to the essence brings rest to discursive攀緣 (pān-yuán) [grasping at conditions];
stripping away appearances halts confusion.
Now, speaking in terms of principle:

This briefly elucidates ten points: first and second, the two kinds of selflessness; second, the explanation of negation (*paryudāsa*); third, being like space; fourth, neither arising nor ceasing; fifth, the absence of self and other; sixth, the absence of conceptual differentiation; seventh, entering non-duality; eighth, the absence of distinction; ninth, clarifying the single flavor; and tenth, returning to the state of total cessation. First, regarding the clarification of the two kinds of selflessness:
This means that for one who can differentiate the characteristics of objects,
those objects being differentiated by that person arise as substantial entities from conditions.
These phenomena, being empty of intrinsic characteristics, appear to exist as mere semblances yet lack substantial reality;
this is precisely what is meant by "the selflessness of persons.
As a sutra says:
Since even a self cannot be apprehended,
how could that which is not-self be apprehended?
Because they arise from sensory objects and conditions, they lack intrinsic nature.
These phenomena are without self.
The treatise states:
"If a phenomenon arises from conditions..."
This is the absence of intrinsic nature;
because both the person and phenomena are without self, they constitute a single flavor.
Second, the explanation of negation (*paryudāsa*).
Question: Are the sense objects existent? Answer: No;
because they arise from conditions and lack intrinsic nature, they are empty.
Question: Are objects non-existent?
Answer: No. This is because they exist as unimpeded dependent origination.
Question: Is the dust both existent and non-existent?
Answer: No. Emptiness sublates existence until it is exhausted, leaving only emptiness.
Because there is the emptiness of being stripped away and the mere existence [of that emptiness], they do not coexist with one another.
Question: Is the object (dharma) neither existent nor non-existent?
Answer: No. This is because there is no obstruction to their coexistence;
both the views of existence and non-existence are eliminated together.
It is not that there are no dharmas.
As the Sūtra says:
"One merely eliminates the illness, but does not eliminate the dharma."
This is the protection against faults.
"The three are like space" means that the substance of dust is empty and non-existent.
It is without limits and cannot be grasped or abandoned,
yet it pervades the ten directions and serves as the basis for all principles, phenomena, understandings, and practices.
Yet it possesses inexhaustible great functions, like space,
serving as the support for all phenomena.
It is established in its entirety,
without boundaries or limits,
pervading throughout the ten directions.
It is just like space;
one thereby attains the wisdom of space, the body of space, and unimpeded function.
Fourth, regarding non-arising and non-ceasing:
This means that as dust arises and disperses from the wind,
it exhibits the characteristics of birth and extinction;
now, let us investigate these characteristics of arising and ceasing.
All are entirely empty and non-existent.
As the Sūtra says:
"By way of causes and conditions, phenomena arise."
Phenomena cease due to causes and conditions;
at the time of their arising, they arise as being without intrinsic nature,
and at the time of their ceasing, they cease as being without intrinsic nature.
Because they lack intrinsic nature, arising is non-arising and cessation is non-cessation.
Fifth, there is no self or other.
This means that objects (viṣaya) are conditions for others,
while the mind (citta) is the cause for itself.
Now, the mind is not [produced] by itself.
It must depend upon conditions;
since it first manifests by means of conditions,
we know this.
They lack intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, objects do not constitute objects of themselves;
they also depend upon the mind.
Since they manifest only through the mind,
one knows that they have no other-nature (parabhāva).
Furthermore, all phenomena are neither self-arisen nor arisen from another.
Therefore, there is neither self nor other.
What is now called "self and other" is not a view of distinct difference.
Self is other-self; other is self-other.
Self and other are of one and the same limit.
This is spoken with sovereign mastery.
The Treatise says:
"Even intrinsic nature does not exist."
Other-nature likewise does not exist.
Regarding the six kinds of non-discrimination:
this refers to seeing the characteristics of objects as being circular or small, beautiful or ugly, or as flying and soaring.
This is the discrimination of one's own mind;
it is precisely this discriminating mind that arises in dependence upon sense objects.
Upon investigation, arising has no substance;
names and characteristics vanish of their own accord.
This is non-conceptualization.
It is simply that when the emotions of conceptual discrimination are destroyed,
it is called "non-discrimination";
it is not like wood or stone.
The Sūtra says:
"Phenomena arise from conceptual discrimination;
they likewise cease through conceptual discrimination."
It is further said:
"Non-conceptual wisdom analyzes without end;
the nature of this endless analysis is the cessation of conceptualization, because conceptualization has no intrinsic substance."
Discrimination is itself non-discrimination;
because it lacks intrinsic nature, it is not obstructed by conditions.
Thus, non-discrimination is itself constant discrimination.
The seventh entry on non-duality means that one perceives objects and the mind as two;
yet these two are in fact non-dual.
If one holds that the object and the mind are one,
it is refuted by stating they are not one;
for what is seen by the deluded mind is not without an objective basis.
If one grasps at objects and mind as two,
it is said that they are not two in order to negate this,
because there are no separate objects apart from the mind.
Because mind and objects are non-dual in their duality,
there is only mind, which lacks intrinsic substance; even oneness is not one.
By means of one, there is no one;
by means of two, there is no two;
one and two are without obstruction.
Manifesting before one, it enters into non-duality.
As the sutra says:
"Within the wisdom of non-duality."
He emerges as a lion among men;
he does not cling to the notions of "one" or "two," for he knows that neither one nor two exists.
The eighth is non-differentiation,
which means that one perceives the characteristics of objects as being circular and minute,
distinct from the boundaries and divisions of all phenomena.
This is the distinction:
one contemplates that objects have no substantiality and are entirely empty;
they are merely manifestations of principle (li) and possess no further distinct entities.
This is without differentiation.
Furthermore, this principle of nature (li-xing) gives rise to all phenomena according to conditions;
it is not without its own distinct boundaries.
This is precisely the distinction.
As the Sūtra says:
"All phenomena are without distinction."
Only the Buddha can discern and know the distinction between phenomena that are differentiated and those that are undifferentiated;
this is because there is no principle or reality that contradicts it.
Nevertheless, although the dependent origination of all phenomena appears as myriad distinctions, the dharma-realm is undifferentiated and is a single emptiness.
Because emptiness and existence are mutually integrated through their identity and difference,
the myriad phenomena are realized as a single emptiness.
Non-differentiation is itself differentiation;
by contemplating the single emptiness, one accomplishes the myriad existents.
Differentiation is itself non-differentiation.
Difference and non-difference manifest as a single limit;
this can be seen through the formulation of the four propositions.
Regarding the ninth, the single flavor of clarity:
This means that objects are established through conditions and are all devoid of intrinsic nature;
although phenomena, principles, teachings, and meanings differ in myriad ways.
There is nothing that is not solely the single flavor of emptiness and stillness;
it is only because of the myriad differences of dependent origination that we speak of the single flavor of emptiness.
If there are no ten thousand differences,
it is this single flavor;
if one brings forth emptiness, then it is simply that the single flavor is only emptiness.
If one raises the perspective of "nature," it is a single flavor that is solely nature;
if one raises the perspective of "suchness," it is a single flavor that is solely suchness.
By analogy, other cases may be understood accordingly.
Regarding "the ten realms are utterly extinguished":
this means that the mind and its objects are mutually extinguished.
If one realizes that objects are manifested solely by the mind, [then they are extinguished].
Then external objects are entirely severed;
if the mind fully manifests objects,
then the internal mind is entirely dissolved.
When they are obliterated, one obliterates the views external to their essence;
when they are preserved, one preserves the phenomena of the complete principle.
Thus, in the very act of obliteration there is constant preservation, and in the very act of preservation there is constant obliteration.
The four propositions can be understood accordingly.
However, the aforementioned meanings are the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), which is difficult to conceive;
mental activities rarely find their scope therein.
The true source is unfathomable; how could names and words ever fathom its beginning?
Yet, though it is wordless, it does not cease speaking;
relying on its essence, it gives rise to its myriad functions, and there is no phenomenon that it does not discern.
It manifests according to conditions;
by means of the single emptiness, phenomena are clarified.
One must necessarily speak of emptiness.
If one speaks of the essence, how could its function not be revealed?
Therefore, when traces are withdrawn, the conditioned mind has no place to rest;
when appearances vanish, deluded consciousness has nothing to rely upon.
Only then can one be said to accord with dependent origination and conform to the Dharma-realm. Chapter Three:
The Door of the Universal Radiance of All-Knowledge (Sarvajñajñāna). Regarding the illumination of great wisdom, one contemplates the ocean of nature within even the finest hair.
When the true source shines forth clearly, one gazes upon the Dharma-body even through a mote of dust;
vast and magnificent like dense clouds,
the one and the many unfold in accordance with responsive manifestations.
The towering peaks and mountain ranges gather principles and phenomena, which differentiate to form shapes.
Now, as they manifest before us in their essence and function,
we shall briefly distinguish ten meanings.

1. Manifesting the extent of reality (*yāvadbhāvikatā*); 2. Dividing the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*); 3. Illuminating the inconceivable; 4. Being born into the family of the Buddha; 5. Displaying the perfect voice; 6. Discerning the primary and secondary [receptacles]; 7. Harmonizing with the resonance of capacities; 8. Performing the Buddha-work; 9. Opening the five eyes; 10. Dividing the three wisdoms. First, manifesting the extent of reality: [The text continues: "The first, manifesting the extent of reality..."
That the substance of objects is empty and non-existent is "in accordance with reality";
that they do not obstruct the vivid manifestation of phenomenal characteristics is likewise so.
This is the measure of reality.
Now, as for the nature of objects:
if they accord with the truth, they are without limits.
All phenomena are entirely manifested based upon the nature; therefore,
within a single atom, one perceives all phenomena.
This matter is the objective realm of the "as-it-is" (yathābhūta) within the wisdom that accords with reality (yathābhūta-jñāna).
Regarding the "two divisions of the six supernormal powers" (ṣaḍabhijñā):
it means that these sensory objects have no intrinsic substance.
Remaining unmoved within the realm of dust,
it constantly pervades the oceans of lands throughout the ten directions,
devoid of any characteristic of coming or going.
This is the supernormal power of the bases of psychic mastery (*ṛddhipāda*). A sūtra states:
"Without rising from one's seat..."
He traveled everywhere throughout the ten directions and further beheld that the dharmadhātu of all phenomena is boundless.
Yet, regarding all principles, phenomena, teachings, and meanings,
they are entirely equal; all bodhisattvas enter into realization together and cultivate them together.
This dharma has no other path; it is the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others.
Furthermore, when the realization and practice of the dharma-realm of perceived objects manifest before one, [this occurs].
He immediately knew that he had previously heard this Dharma in the presence of a Buddha,
because his contemplation of the mind was uninterrupted.
Therefore, what has been attained today constitutes the supernormal power of knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*).
Furthermore, one perceives that the nature of sensory objects is empty and quiescent, such that no characteristic can be apprehended.
This is precisely the absence of dualistic views.
If one perceives characteristics, that constitutes dualistic views;
because there are no characteristics, there is no duality.
This is called the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*). A sutra states:
"To see without the two marks is called the true divine eye."
Furthermore, when one realizes that objects are unborn,
devoid of intrinsic nature, empty,
and quiescent, the grasping mind does not arise.
This is the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*). A sutra says:
"Severing the fetters and emptying the mind."
I am thus without birth. Furthermore,
upon hearing the sounds that distinguish the realms of sensory objects and the dharma-realm,
I immediately know them.
All sounds are entirely the ear and can no longer be heard as objects.
Yet this hearing is without conditions and without attainment;
through sound, one awakens to all dharmas.
Constantly hearing all Buddha-dharmas is the supernormal power of the divine ear.
Regarding the "inconceivable three knowledges":
This means that while the objects do not lose their minute dimensions,
they appear therein, pervading the ten directions and universally encompassing all things.
This arises because valid cognition is itself non-valid cognition, and non-valid cognition is itself valid cognition.
Furthermore, that which dwells within the realm of seeing and hearing is precisely beyond the reach of seeing and hearing.
When one dwells at the limit of conceptualization,
that very conceptualization becomes unfathomable;
this is because the inconceivable essence itself cannot be apprehended.
This is precisely the unthinkable within thought.
As a sutra says:
"That which is thought is the unthinkable."
This is called "inconceivable.
Regarding those who are born into the Buddha-family:
the Buddha takes the principle of non-arising within the *tathatā* dharma-realm as his family.
Now, when one perceives that sensory objects are without arising and without intrinsic nature,
this very wisdom manifests from the dharma of non-arising; therefore,
it is called "being born into the family of the Buddhas."
The Sūtra says:
"To be non-discriminative regarding phenomena is to be born from Suchness."
It is further said:
"If one universally realizes non-arising within the Buddha-dharma of the three periods of time,
and is born through transformation merely by acceding to its principles and meanings, one is then said to be born into the family of the Buddha."
These are the sons of the Buddha;
they are also called the manifestation of the Buddha. According to another version, it says:
"The principle of non-arising—bodhi and nirvāṇa—is their home."
Fifth, regarding the manifestation of the perfect voice:
this refers to the sound that speaks of the sensory objects;
yet this voice is fully endowed with the treasury of wisdom.
According to the capacities of sentient beings,
there are varying degrees of resonance;
this is the case with respect to sound.
Because one realizes that large and small phonemes are merely provisional designations, empty, and non-existent;
yet, to hold that sound is real is the disposition of those with the capacity of the Hīnayāna.
This is precisely what is revealed by the teachings for the ignorant.
Within sound itself, one realizes that the phenomenon of sound has no intrinsic substance.
This is how phenomena are integrated to reveal the principle.
This arises from the capacity for the Mahāyāna,
which is the manifestation of the Final Teaching (Zhōngjiào).
Within sounds, one immediately realizes that all sounds, whether great or small, are empty and non-existent.
To give rise to a thought or stir a念 (nian) is to deviate from the essence of the Dharma.
That which is of a single flavor and a single characteristic, beyond all discrimination,
is the spiritual capacity for the Mahāyāna.
This is the manifestation of the Sudden Teaching (*dun-jiao*).

Within sounds, one thoroughly understands that sound is the *dharmadhātu* of dependent origination, wherein bodhi and nirvāṇa are sovereign in their primary and attendant aspects. One is all, and all is one.
It is like the infinite realms of the pearl nets in Indra’s palace, layer upon layer;
this is manifested by the One Vehicle according to the capacities of sentient beings,
which is precisely the teaching of the Perfect School.
Above this single sound,
because the capacities of sentient beings vary between great and small,
this Dharma-gate likewise does not remain uniform.
All sounds, each and every one being thus,
constitute the Tathāgata’s unimpeded, perfect voice, the wheel of Dharma which turns eternally.
Sixth, the distinction between the environment and its inhabitants:
this means that the oceans of lands within the dust motes are the environment (āśraya),
while the Buddha’s body, wisdom, and radiance are the inhabitants (adhiṣṭhāna).
Now, these atoms are manifested by the Buddha's wisdom;
their entire substance is entirely the Buddha's wisdom.
Therefore, within the radiance, one perceives the subtle dust-like Buddha-fields.
Furthermore, the atoms within the ocean of lands take the entire nature of the Dharma-realm as the substance of their atomic bodies.
Therefore, one sees within the sensory objects all such matters as the Buddhas preaching the Dharma and manifesting through transformational birth;
one should know that the support is itself the supported, and the supported is itself the support.
They are sovereign and unimpeded;
even down to the smallest speck of dust, a single hair, or a world-system—
each and every phenomenon is likewise so.

This refers to the entirety of the Buddhas' reliance on both the Dharma and its physical manifestation. Regarding the "responsive resonance of the seven assemblies," it means that the sensory objects are the suchness of the equal Dharma-realm.
They are manifested according to wisdom:
when the capacity of the recipient is great, the manifestation of the meaning is also great;
when the capacity is small, the manifestation of the principle is also small.
According to the faculties and natures of sentient beings,
there are varying depths of realization;
this constitutes the resonance between capacity and response.
This very responsive resonance is the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body in its entirety. Eighth,
the performance of Buddha-activities through giving:
This means that sensory objects, sounds, and written characters are all devoid of intrinsic nature; because they are thus, they are liberation.
These are characters without intrinsic nature.
It is the non-activity of activity,
because it is empty and non-existent;
it is that which is revealed by the Buddha's wisdom.
Whatever actions one performs,
as long as they do not lose the dharma-realm,
they constitute the work of a Buddha.
The Sūtra says:
"Whatever actions one performs,
none are not the work of the Buddha."
Regarding the opening of the five eyes:
form, which is devoid of intrinsic nature, is the fleshly eye;
phenomena, which are dependently originated, are the Dharma eye.
Because the nature of sensory objects is empty, they are non-existent; this is the wisdom-eye.
Sensory objects have no marks that can be apprehended;
all conceptual discriminations are stilled.
Because it is free from dualistic views, it is called the "divine eye.
The nature of sensory objects is empty and quiescent;
no characteristics can be apprehended.
The non-obstruction between the primary and secondary realms, the perfect fusion of thought-moments and eons, and the equality of existence and non-existence—
this is called the Buddha-eye.
However, one cannot perceive objects through the five eyes.
However, names are established according to what appears within the realm of sensory objects (*viṣaya*).
As for the "threefold wisdom regarding the ten [realms]," it refers to the realization of the principle that the nature of sensory objects is empty and non-existent.
Discriminating between the heterodox and the orthodox,
one accords with principle and enters the truth;
this is the mind of discernment.
This is the wisdom of preparatory application (*prayoga-jñāna*).
Furthermore, one sees that these objects are entirely beyond words and transcendent of thought;
their nature exceeds all calculation, such that subject and object do not arise, and even the movement of thought is neither present nor absent.
This is the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Furthermore, one perceives that the objects of perception arise as illusory existents through dependent origination without obstructing their distinctness;
yet, despite these manifold distinctions, they are all empty and non-existent.
Because its essence is not lost,
the great function arises entirely from the essence of the Dharma;
unity and multiplicity are unimpeded, and the principal and its associates mutually encompass one another.
One is all; all is one. This is subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna).
However, the dharmas of the various meanings mentioned above have no fixed boundaries;
they necessarily manifest simultaneously, for logically there is no obstruction to their differentiation,
and their concealment and manifestation share a single limit.
When in operation, it surges like billowing waves and boils like a cauldron,
functioning by means of the complete True Body; when in its essential nature,
it is as clear as a mirror and as limpid as still water.
Arising in accordance with conditions yet converging in stillness;
like the radiance of the sun’s rays, it is without intentionality,
yet illuminates the ten directions.
Like the surface of a clear mirror, forms appear in their myriad manifestations without moving. 4.
The Gate of Melted Fusion and Spontaneous Functioning. Fourth: Now, the ocean of nature is boundless.
By means of this, manifold virtues flourish and expand;
the inconceivable many gateways of dependent origination thereby become perfectly integrated.
There is nothing that does not revolve through the myriad differences of forms that contract and unfold.
Following the momentum of wisdom’s melting and fusing into a single boundary,
the power of non-arising illumination proceeds from the mind;
though manifesting in differentiation, it always accords with its function without ever deviating from its essence.
Although it is of a single flavor and ever-pervasive,
if we speak in terms of its essential nature and manifestations,
it may be briefly divided into ten meanings.

1. Harmonizing Principle and Phenomena; 2. Penetrating Form and Emptiness; 3. Mastering the Great and Small; 4. Integrating the Distant and Near; 5. Clarifying the Pure and Mixed; 6. Fusing Thought-moments and Eons; 7. Realizing the One and the Many; 8. Harmonizing the Comprehensive and the Limited; 9. Clarifying Reversion and Expansion; 10. Total Perfect Fusion. First, harmonizing principle and phenomena: [The text continues with the detailed explanation of these ten points.]
That the characteristics of a particle are circular and minute is a matter of fact;
that the nature of the particle is empty and non-existent is a principle.
This is because the phenomenon has no substantial essence.
Phenomena are harmoniously integrated according to principle;
because sensory objects lack intrinsic substance,
they immediately and universally pervade all things.
Because every phenomenon does not differ from principle,
it manifests entirely within the sensory objects;
thus, the Sūtra says:
The vast world is itself the narrow world;
the narrow world is itself the vast world.
Those who realize that both are empty of inherent nature [perceive] form as emptiness.
Just as one perceives that dust arises and is established through conditions, so too is form;
because form has no intrinsic substance, it is empty.
If emptiness were devoid of form, one could not speak of it as "empty."
This means that there is no false form of the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya);
it is because of false form that the true emptiness of ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) exists.
If form were not empty, one could speak of form.
This is the true emptiness that is devoid of any ultimate truth;
because of this true emptiness, there exists the delusory form of conventional truth.
Now, one need only realize that these delusions have no substantial essence.
This is precisely true emptiness;
it is not that the absence of form is called emptiness.
As the Sūtra says:
The nature of form is itself empty;
it is not that form must cease for it to be empty.
This third point applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
For example, the circular form of a mote of dust is small,
while Mount Sumeru, with its height and breadth, is large;
yet this mote of dust and that mountain [are both empty].
Large and small interpenetrate;
they revolve according to the mind,
yet are neither born nor extinguished.
Furthermore, for instance, when one perceives something as high and vast,
it is merely the manifestation of one's own mind appearing as large;
there is no separate "large" entity existing apart from that.
Now, when one perceives a speck of dust as small and round,
this too is merely the manifestation of one's own mind as small;
there is no "small" apart from that.
Now, due to seeing the object,
one perceives the mountain in its entirety with a mind that grasps it as high and vast.
Yet it manifests as sensory objects.
Therefore, the small can contain the large.
As the Sūtra says:
Countless vajra-circles of Mount Cakravāḍa can all be placed upon a single hair-tip;
this is to clarify that within the ultimate great there are small characteristics.
The bodhisattva initiates the first resolve because of this.
Regarding the fourth point, "gathering those far and near":
it means that these sensory objects are near.
Those worlds of the ten directions are distant;
yet now, these particles have no inherent substance,
pervading all throughout the ten directions.
Thus, these ten directions, which are entirely composed of particles,
are such that the distant is always near. Nevertheless,
although the ten directions are distant...
It is merely the ten directions of the nature of dust;
even if one transcends unspeakably many worlds,
one still does not go beyond the nature of dust.
Why is this? Because the measure of atoms has no intrinsic substance;
it is equal to the realm of empty space.
Because it cannot transcend [this],
therefore throughout all the ten directions,
only the nature of the dust (dust-essence) is manifest.
Furthermore, even though one has departed from here and reached the ten directions,
one still perceives these objects. Why is this?
Because sensory objects lack intrinsic substance,
phenomena manifest in accordance with principle;
therefore, the nature of sensory objects—
At all times, sensory objects likewise appear in this same manner;
thus, within a single atom, all things are manifested.
Yet distance and proximity, self and other, remain distinct;
the ten directions enter into a single atom,
remaining distant while eternally near.
Dust pervades the ten directions;
though near, it is ever distant.
Dust and the ten directions—[are they one or different?]
The near and the far are clearly of one and the same limit;
contemplate this further, that there is no distinction between them.
Regarding the fivefold purity and impurity:
"the non-arising of objects" means that all phenomena are without arising; this is purity.
Within the meaning of the non-arising of sensory objects,
both principle and phenomena are fully contained;
thus, being both emptiness and form, both bodhi and nirvana, and so forth, constitutes their interpenetration.
Principle does not obstruct phenomena;
it is purely constant yet intermingled with them.
Phenomena are constantly complete within principle.
"Miscellaneous" (*za*) means "constant" (*heng*) and "pure" (*chun*).
Because of the mastery over both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*),
purity and mixture are without obstruction.
Regarding the sixfold fusion of thought-moments and kalpas:
for example, when perceiving a speck of dust,
it is manifested by a single thought-moment of mind.
When this single thought-moment manifests,
it is entirely composed of hundreds of thousands of great eons. Why is this?
It is through a hundred thousand great kalpas, originating from a single initial thought, that a great kalpa is finally established;
yet once they are thus established,
both are devoid of intrinsic nature.
Because a single thought-moment lacks intrinsic nature,
it immediately pervades a great kalpa; likewise,
the great kalpa lacks intrinsic nature.
It is precisely this single thought-moment;
because both thought and eons lack inherent substance,
the characteristics of long and short naturally merge.
Extending even to distant and near worlds,
including all Buddhas and sentient beings,
as well as all phenomena throughout the three periods of time.
There is nothing that does not manifest within a single thought-moment.
Why is this? Because all phenomena and events...
They manifest in dependence upon the mind;
once mindfulness is unimpeded,
phenomena likewise dissolve accordingly.
Therefore, in a single thought-moment, all phenomena of the three periods of time are clearly perceived.
As a sutra says:
"A single thought-moment may be a hundred thousand kalpas."
A hundred thousand kalpas are but a single thought-moment.
Regarding the resolution of the many and the one:
for example, the self-characteristic of a mote of dust is one.
Only by remaining unmoved within its own singularity can it universally manifest as many; if it were to move from its own singularity, [it could not do so].
Thus, the universal application is lost;
even the "many" is not established.
The same applies to one, two, and three as well.
Furthermore, the establishment of the one and the many is mutually dependent:
for instance, it is only when the one is entirely composed of the many that it can be called "one."
Furthermore, it is precisely because many are identical that they are called "many";
apart from the many, there is no separate "one."
One clearly knows that this "many" is one among many;
apart from the one, there is no separate "many."
One clearly knows that within the one there are many;
this is precisely because it is not many.
Nevertheless, it can manifest as one or many;
though not one, it can manifest as many or one,
because it does not lose its lack of intrinsic nature.
Only then does the wisdom of "one" and "many" arise.
As the Sūtra says:
"It is like the method of calculation, which increases from one up to ten."
Up to the point where there is no measure, all arise from the fundamental number; thus, wisdom is without distinction.
Regarding the eight assemblies, they are both universal and specific.
That is to say, the minor characteristics of sensory objects are localized,
whereas the absence of intrinsic nature in those characteristics is universal; thus,
there are now infinite oceans of lands.
To constantly manifest within a single mote of dust is to be pervasive while remaining localized;

for a single mote of dust to fully pervade the ocean of lands is to be localized while remaining pervasive. Furthermore, to contain the vast within the minute without destroying its smallness is the inconceivable.
A single atom can extensively contain a Buddha-field;
without diminishing its vastness, it dwells within the minute—
this is the inconceivable.
The oceans of Buddha-fields constantly appear within a single atom;
this is what is meant by the non-obstruction between the pervasive and the localized.
Ninth, the clarification of expansion and contraction:
This means that because objects have no inherent nature, their entire substance pervades the ten directions; this is "extension.
Because the ten directions have no substantiality, they manifest entirely within objects according to conditions; this is "contraction.
As the Sūtra says:
A single buddha-land fills the ten directions,
and the ten directions enter into one without remainder.
Now, when this scroll is unrolled, all phenomena appear within a single atom.
If it is extended, then a single atom pervades all places; thus, while always extended, it is always coiled.
Because a single atom encompasses all things, while always coiled, it is always extended.
Because all things are subsumed within a single atom,
this is what is meant by mastery over contraction and expansion.
As for the tenth point, "total interpenetration":
This means that once the characteristics of objects have been exhausted and deluded consciousness has also ceased—
because phenomena lack inherent substance—
phenomena accord with principle and become perfectly interfused.
Because the substance consists of phenomena,
the principle accords with phenomena to achieve comprehensive realization;
thus, though there is existence all day long, it is eternally empty.
Emptiness does not sever existence;
though it is empty all day long, existence is ever-present.
Existence does not obstruct emptiness.
Yet, existence that does not obstruct emptiness can harmonize all phenomena;
emptiness that does not sever existence [remains ever-present].
It can accomplish all things;
therefore, the myriad phenomena appear vividly,
with no obstruction between this and that.
However, the tendency for the various meanings above to melt and fuse arises through the realization of the absence of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva),
which allows them to function spontaneously.
Through the arising of causes and conditions, they are brought into assembly;
the one and the many are fully encompassed within a single speck of dust,
and thus it is suddenly revealed.
As they mutually encompass one another, even the finest hairs appear simultaneously;
this is because when the mind is penetrating, the dharma-gates are sovereign,
and when the meaning is manifest, great wisdom is thereby accomplished.
Those who seek it find it difficult to exhaust its source;
those who discuss it rarely fathom its profundity.
It is the functioning of spontaneous movement.
How can it be described? Section Five:
The Gate of the Manifestation of Essence and Function. Now, the essence of the Dharma is perfectly pervasive, its true source complete and penetrating.
When manifested, it clearly illuminates the ten directions.
Thus, all things are fully revealed:
by pointing to a single mote of dust, one beholds the sublime mystery;
by lifting a mere hair, one contemplates the realm of the Buddha. Now, delusion is penetrated and truth is disclosed.

Briefly divided, there are ten meanings: first, manifesting radiance; second, understanding the object and the wisdom; third, clarifying the causes of birth and arising; fourth, clarifying the realm of the Buddha; fifth, distinguishing cause and effect; sixth, clarifying the Buddha-nature; seventh, expressing the virtues of nature; eighth, the manifestation of one's own mind; ninth, the supramundane; tenth, relying on birth for liberation. First, regarding the manifestation of radiance:
This refers to when, upon seeing the dharmadhātu-tathatā— the principle within phenomena—
it is revealed with perfect clarity;
this is the illumination of the light of wisdom.
If there is no light of wisdom,
then principle and phenomena will not be revealed; it is only when one perceives the dharmas that [they become manifest].
This mind is luminous;
because its accumulation of wisdom has reached perfection,
it therefore emits a single ray of light.
Thus, there is nothing in the dharma-realm that is not revealed.
Constantly observing the entire dharma-realm is what is meant by emitting light that illumines all.
Second, regarding the wisdom that cognizes objects:
for example, the circular and minute phenomenal characteristics of a single atom are the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
to cognize that the atom is without arising and without intrinsic nature is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Those two truths, the ultimate and the conventional,
are the objects upon which one relies;
this is the mind that penetrates them through and through.
This is the wisdom that relies upon [the ultimate]. Regarding its object,
this wisdom no longer possesses the two kinds of conceptual discrimination between grasper and grasped.
Why is this? It is only when wisdom is now accomplished through the Dharma that it can be called "wisdom."
Apart from phenomena, there is no wisdom capable of discerning them.
Only when phenomena are manifested through wisdom can they be spoken of.
The Dharma is detached from cognition and thus has no object of conceptual discrimination.
Because the mind and its objects are quiescent,
it remains ever serene despite its pervasive illumination.
Because phenomena follow conditions,
they are constantly functional despite being empty and quiescent.
Third, regarding the cause that produces arising:
This refers to the meaning of the dharma-realm of dependent origination, wherein the substance of sensory objects is empty and quiescent;
it is manifested only through wisdom, and thus wisdom is the "revealing cause" (jñāna-hetu).
Having perceived the essence of the objects, one cultivates the stage of practice through understanding;
this gives rise to functional power,
which is the cause of birth.
Yet arising is itself non-arising,
which is identical to the essence of phenomena;
even comprehension is not comprehension.
How could it be that arising from equal conditions and the act of cognizing are without distinction?
"Arising" refers to activity;
"realizing" refers to the essence.
Non-essence is itself the essence.
When fully understood, there is no arising;
its essence is itself essence-less.
Arising, in turn, is for the sake of understanding.
The realization is identical to the single limit;
there is no differentiation.
Regarding the fourth clarification of the Buddha’s realm:
This means that the substance of the object cannot be apprehended.
This non-apprehension is the Buddha’s attainment of the characteristic of objects as being without limits and without anything upon which to rely.
This is non-reliance;
it is the Buddha’s reliance on the fact that the substance of objects does not arise.
This non-arising is the Buddha’s arising, which is non-discriminative regarding objects.
This is the Buddha’s analytical exposition:
it is precisely through non-attainment, non-reliance,
and non-arising that one is able to establish all phenomena.
Furthermore, it is impossible for the entirety of an object to be seen and yet remain unseen, or even to be heard and yet remain unheard;
all such instances are the Buddha’s seeing and hearing.
As a sutra says:
That which is seen cannot be seen;
that which is heard cannot be heard.
This is the fivefold eloquence regarding cause and effect.
Dust is the cause, appearing as the manifest phenomena of dependent origination;
that the substance of these phenomena is empty and ungraspable is the result.
The result is not different from the cause.
The cause is designated as the fruit because it is entirely fulfilled;
since the cause is not distinct from the fruit,
the fruit is designated as the cause because it is entirely perfected.
If the cause does not obtain the fruit,
then the fruit is not a fruit; if the fruit does not obtain the cause, [it is likewise not a fruit].
The cause is also not a cause,
for they are all established simultaneously without distinction. Therefore,
at the moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment (prathamacittotpāda),...
He immediately attained perfect enlightenment.
Having attained perfect enlightenment,
this was indeed his initial resolve.
The Sūtra says:
"At the very moment of first generating the mind [of enlightenment], one immediately attains perfect awakening,
becoming equal to all the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time."
Sixth, regarding the clarification of Buddha-nature:
it refers to awakening to the fact that both sense objects and all phenomena lack intrinsic nature because they arise from conditions; this is called Buddha-nature.
The Sūtra says:
"The seeds of the Buddhas of the three periods of time take non-nature as their nature."
This applies to all places:
to realize that there is no intrinsic nature is itself buddha-nature;
it does not exist because of sentient beings.
It is not because they are insentient that they do not exist;
the reason for speaking now specifically of "sentient beings" is the intention to exhort people to become worthy vessels.
Constantly, within a single speck of dust or a single hair’s breadth,
one clearly perceives that all principles and phenomena are none other than the nature of the Tathāgata.
The manifestation and development of the Tathāgata’s nature-arising merit is called Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
Seventh, regarding the manifesting qualities of nature (*prakṛtiguṇa*):
Question: Are the sense objects (*viṣaya*) existent?
The answer is: it is the existence of that which does not exist, like the moon in water or a reflection in a mirror.
As the Sūtra says:
"That which is not existent is existence.
Question: "Are objects non-existent?
Answer: "They are the non-existence of existence; they are empty of intrinsic nature."
The Sūtra says:
"Existence is not existence.
Question: Are the sensory objects both existent and non-existent?
Answer: It exists because it arises from conditions;
it is empty because it lacks intrinsic nature.
Thus, emptiness and existence are of one and the same limit, established with sovereign mastery.
The Treatise says:
"Because the meaning of emptiness exists,
all phenomena are established."
Question: Are objects neither existent nor non-existent?
Answer: Both the characteristic of existence and the characteristic of emptiness are unapprehendable;
they mutually cancel each other out until both are exhausted.
There is nothing established.
This present nature-virtue is simply free from attachment.
It does not obstruct conceptual discrimination.
The treatise says:
"If [one holds that] existence and non-existence are both negated and affirmed, then it should also apply [to the other]."
Listening while remaining free from speech and with a mind unattached—
this is without fault. Eighth,
clarifying that which is manifested by one's own mind.
Just as when these objects are seen, they are manifestations of one's own mind;
now that these objects have manifested from the mind,
they in turn serve as conditions for that very same mind.
Ultimately, there are no phenomena external to the mind that can serve as objects for the mind,
because they do not exist externally.
One should understand that these objects are merely manifestations of one's own mind;
apart from the mind,
not a single dharma exists.
Even if one perceives the internal and external,
these are merely manifestations of one's own mind;
there is no separate internal or external.
This is not an error. Regarding the nine supramundane [perceptions]:
it refers to perceiving the forms and characteristics of sensory objects and forming a conception of them as real.
This is abiding in the world;
now, that the marks of dust are empty and non-existent,
this is transcending the world.
The Sūtra states:
"The phenomena of the five aggregates throughout the three periods of time are called the world;
this arises from false existence."
Non-conceptualization is that which transcends the world.
Regarding the ten ways of generating understanding by relying on phenomena:
it is like perceiving the marks of sensory objects.
When this matter is thoroughly penetrated within the context of phenomena,
the principle of non-arising manifests before one;
this is called "giving rise to understanding by relying on phenomena."
Furthermore, external objects are separately relied upon to symbolize this dharma.
This is because the dharma of the object is sovereign;
it is by means of the object that it is symbolized, manifesting the dharma’s moistening and benefiting power.
It is represented by clouds and rain to manifest that the nature and virtues of the dust-like phenomena are profound and vast;
it is represented by the ocean.
Thus they are immeasurable;
furthermore, there are other things signified,
each of which is distinct.
When one investigates this through wisdom,
the various meanings mentioned above show that once delusion is exhausted and wisdom arises, appearances vanish and the essence is revealed.
Through the dependent origination of differentiation,
the waves of the ocean of nature surge forth;
this single-flavor true source is the ultimate origin.
By using this to manifest the mirror that accords with conditions,
the Way of realizing truth is lost;
how far removed it becomes!
6. The Section on the Manifestation of Distinctions, the Sixth. Now, the fulfillment of the teaching is inconceivable;
by observing a single speck of dust, it manifests instantaneously.
The perfect school is unfathomable.
Upon observing even a single hair’s breadth, it is suddenly revealed;
yet, as function accords with essence,
there is no lack of the momentum of differentiation.
Phenomena manifest based on principle;
they inherently possess a singular boundary.
For now, I shall briefly set forth the general outline.

This reveals ten meanings: first, elucidating *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; second, opening up the two truths; third, entering and emerging from meditative absorption; fourth, penetrating the arising of nature; fifth, distinguishing the six characteristics; sixth, manifesting the Indra’s net; seventh, discerning the subtle; eighth, penetrating the inverse and the direct; ninth, determining the principal and the attendant; tenth, ascending to the other shore. First, regarding the elucidation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*: *Śamatha* (calm abiding) is the cessation of all mental activity, while *vipaśyanā* (insight) is the illumination of all phenomena. Because the mind is tranquil, it is called "calm abiding"; because wisdom is clear, it is called "insight. Furthermore, because the mind is quiescent, it is called "calm abiding"; because wisdom is luminous, it is called "insight. Moreover, because the mind is non-arising, it is called "calm abiding"; because wisdom is non-obscured, it is called "insight. Additionally, because the mind is unconditioned, it is called "calm abiding"; because wisdom is unimpeded, it is called "insight. Furthermore, because the mind is non-discriminatory, it is called "calm abiding"; because wisdom is non-delusive, it is called "insight. Also, because the mind is non-grasping, it is called "calm abiding"; because wisdom is non-forgetting, it is called "insight. Moreover, because the mind is non-conceptual, it is called "calm abiding"; because wisdom is non-obscured, it is called "insight. Furthermore, because the mind is non-differentiation, it is called "calm abiding"; because wisdom is non-attachment, it is called "insight. Additionally, because the mind is non-abiding, it is called "calm abiding"; because wisdom is non-retrogression, it is called "insight. Moreover, because the mind is non-dwelling, it is called "calm abiding"; because wisdom is non-destruction, it is called "insight. First, distinguishing right view: [The text continues with the detailed explanation of the first section.]
To see the names and marks of objects as real is erroneous;

This is not correct,
because it does not see by seeing the object.
This, too, is not correct.
One simply knows that the objects are entirely the seeing itself;
one no longer sees anything further,
because one does not see the seeing as being within the objects.
However, when seeing these objects,
one does not see them with the wisdom-eye, nor view them with the dharma-eye, nor observe them with the buddha-eye, nor look at them with the flesh-eye, nor gaze upon them with the deva-eye.

that is to say, to see by means of seeing is not to accord with sensory objects.

meaning that one further uses non-seeing to perceive objects—
one likewise fails to accord with those objects.
If one does not see, then one simply does not see;

If one sees, it is truly seeing.
This means that only when one knows that the objects are entirely the seeing itself can it be called "seeing."
The Sūtra says:
"The one who sees is defilement;
that [which is seen] is without anything seen."
All Buddhas are free from that which is seen;
therefore, their vision is pure.
Second, the discernment of defilement and purity:
This means that seeing the arising and ceasing, existence and non-existence of objects is defilement;
whereas the essence itself, which is neither arising nor ceasing, neither existent nor non-existent, is purity.
If emptiness were different from existence, [it would not be purity].
Then purity would not be called pure,
because it is deluded regarding emptiness;
for if there were something distinct from emptiness, [it could not be pure].
Then defilement cannot be called "defilement," because one clings to its existence;
yet that which currently exists is entirely empty.
Only then is it called the defiled portion;
when emptiness is entirely present,

there is mastery over defilement and purity.
As the Sūtra says:
Being stained yet unstained;
being unstained yet stained.
These three reveal the absence of a knower.

Each is unaware of the others.

now the Tathāgata has appeared.
It is entirely because the sensory objects lack intrinsic nature that the dharmadhātu, dependent origination, bodhi,
and nirvāṇa constitute the body of the Tathāgata.

therefore, it extends to all lands, all sentient beings, and all phenomena.
All dependent origination,
all karmic retributions,
and all atoms, hairs, and so forth.

such as bodhi, nirvāṇa, and so forth.

this refers to those who, amidst sensory objects, do not understand that they are their own minds.

from this craving and karma, retribution is formed.

just like a snake [perceived] upon a rope.

The snake is the deluded mind;
it is falsely conceived as existing,

Yet, as for this awakening and this delusion—
